title: Effects of Obstructive Sleep Apnea Treatment on Cardiovascular and Sleep Health in Same-Bed Sleep Partners: The SLEEP PARTNERS Randomized Trial
journal: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine

sections.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> <jats:p>RATIONALE: Previous evidence suggests that obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with impaired sleep quality in same-bed sleep partners (SBSP). However, it is unknown whether OSA affects cardiovascular parameters in SBSP. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of 3 months of OSA treatment on cardiovascular and sleep health of SBSP. METHODS: In this placebo-controlled trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03011294), we randomly assigned patients with moderate/severe OSA (apnea-hypopnea index ≥15 events/h) who had SBSP to receive continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or placebo (nasal strips). We excluded SBSP under OSA treatment or previous history of cardiovascular events. At baseline and after 3-months of follow-up, SBSP underwent a clinical evaluation, sleep questionnaires, objective sleep duration and fragmentation using a 1-week wrist actigraphy, endothelial function (flow-mediated dilation, FMD) and 24-h ambulatory blood pressure (BP) monitoring (ABPM). Primary endpoint: endothelial function; secondary endpoints: ABPM and sleep parameters. RESULTS: Sixty-three SBSP were included in the final analysis (age: 48±10 years; 79% women). At baseline, we noted significant impairments in FMD (3.2% [-0.1, 6.7]), and 50% exhibited a systolic non-dipping BP pattern. We also observed sleep health impairments in SBSP, including long sleep latency (38.2±26.5 minutes), sleep fragmentation (34.1±11.0 awakenings), <7-hours sleep duration (6.4±1.0 hours), and poor sleep quality (63%). Additionally, 24% had moderate/severe OSA. Mean adherence to CPAP and nasal strips in the partners were 5.7±1.8 h/night and 93.1±12.6%, respectively. Compared to placebo, 3-months of CPAP promoted no significant delta differences in FMD (Δ:-0.94% [6.03,2.24] vs. Δ:-3.27% [-6.50,1.76], P=0.67). Stratified analysis excluding SBSP with moderate/severe OSA did not change the primary outcome. However, ABPM data revealed significant delta differences in 24-h systolic BP (CPAP: -0.85±5.22mmHg; placebo: +3.14±8.00mmHg; P=0.03), and daytime systolic BP (CPAP: -1.21±5.51mmHg; placebo: +3.82±8.85mmHg; P=0.01). These BP results remained consistent after excluding SBSP with moderate/severe OSA, with a trend towards significance for nighttime systolic BP (CPAP: -1.10±6.18mmHg; placebo: +3.11±8.60mmHg; P=0.05). CPAP significantly improved sleep quality (P=0.02) and reduced excessive daytime sleepiness (P=0.01) in SBSP. Compared to placebo, CPAP showed significant delta differences in wake after sleep onset (Δ:+7.36±17.51minutes vs. Δ:-4.71±20.32minutes, respectively, P=0.002) and the number of awakenings (Δ:+2.83±9.14 vs. Δ:-0.97±9.42, respectively, P=0.02). These improvements in sleep quality were consistent even after excluding SBSP with moderate/severe OSA (P<0.05 for all comparisons). CONCLUSIONS: In SBSP of patients with moderate/severe OSA, 3-months of CPAP therapy promoted no significant improvement on endothelial function, but prevented BP increase alongside improvements in sleep quality and fragmentation.</jats:p>
